endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, ascertain whether there is a protocol for disclosure of errors or hallucinations, accompanied by an explanation of implications for users.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a protocol for disclosing identified AI errors or hallucinations, with an explanation of clinical implications, reduces continued reliance on affected outputs. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, and no study was supplied that documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation therefore reflects expert consensus from one framework rather than measured effects on user behavior or patient outcomes.

The only supporting source is the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, a voluntary assurance framework that lists an error disclosure protocol as a must. No statute, rule, or regulatory standard appears among the supplied endorsements, so adoption depends on organizational policy rather than a supplied legal requirement.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare settings with and without a formal error disclosure protocol and measure whether clinicians and patients stop relying on outputs affected by known AI errors, how quickly disclosures reach users, whether explanations of clinical implications are understood, and whether downstream harm changes. Basic descriptive work is also needed to establish how often users continue to act on outputs after an error has been identified.
commentary.underserved_note: No study was supplied, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether disclosures and explanations of clinical implications reach and are understood by these groups remains untested, and organizations serving them have no evidence on which disclosure formats or languages work.
